title: How to choose a smartphone in 2026
lead: Most phones are good enough today. The real differences are battery life, years of updates, camera range and size. Here is how to weigh them.

p: Write down what you actually do on your phone. Messaging, maps, banking and video calls run well on almost any mid-range model. Heavy mobile gaming, lots of video recording, or using the phone as your only camera are the cases where flagship hardware pays off.

Then decide on size. Phones with a 6.1–6.3 inch screen are easy to use with one hand and usually weigh 170–190 g. Models with 6.7 inches or more are better for video and reading, but often weigh 210–230 g and do not fit every pocket. Hold one in a shop before you commit.
Finally, pick your ecosystem. If you already use a smartwatch, earbuds or a laptop from one platform, switching costs time and sometimes money. That is a fair reason to stay.

A phone is only safe while it receives security patches. In 2026 the best manufacturers promise 6–7 years of OS and security updates, and EU ecodesign rules now require at least 5 years of updates after the last unit of a model is sold in the EU.

Check the official update policy for the exact model, not the brand in general. Budget lines often get fewer years than flagships from the same company. A phone with 7 years of support can easily outlast two cheaper ones.

Updates also keep your apps working. Banking, payment and messaging apps gradually drop support for older Android and iOS versions, so a phone that stops receiving updates can lose key apps even while the hardware still runs fine.

Battery capacity in mAh is a rough guide only. Efficiency of the chipset and screen matters as much. As a rule of thumb, 4,500–5,000 mAh lasts a full day of mixed use in most phones, and new silicon-carbon batteries now put 5,500–7,000 mAh into normal-sized bodies.

Charging speed above 45–65 W saves only a few minutes in practice. Wireless charging at 15 W or more and Qi2 magnetic alignment are more useful day to day. Look for a battery-care setting that stops charging at 80%; it noticeably extends battery lifespan.
An OLED panel with a 120 Hz refresh rate is now standard above the entry level and is worth having. Scrolling looks smoother and LTPO panels can drop to 1–10 Hz to save power.

For outdoor use, look at measured peak brightness: 1,500 nits or more stays readable in direct summer sun. If you are sensitive to flicker, check whether the screen uses high-frequency PWM dimming (1,920 Hz or above) or DC-like dimming.
Screen size and screen quality are separate choices. A compact phone can have the same top-tier panel as a large one, so do not assume you must go big to get the best display.

Any current flagship chip is faster than you need. Mid-range chips handle everyday apps fine, but on-device AI features increasingly need more memory. Aim for 8 GB of RAM as a minimum and 12 GB if you want to keep the phone 5 years or more.
Storage cannot be upgraded on most phones, because memory card slots have almost disappeared. 128 GB is tight if you shoot 4K video; 256 GB is the safe choice for most people.
Ignore the megapixel race. A 50 MP main sensor is common across price tiers, and larger sensor size matters more than pixel count for low-light photos.

The biggest real-world difference is a telephoto lens. A 3× or 5× optical zoom (often a periscope) makes portraits and distant subjects far sharper than digital cropping. An ultrawide camera is useful for rooms and landscapes; a separate 2 MP macro or depth camera adds almost nothing.
Benchmark scores, "AI" labels on the box and 100+ MP headlines do not tell you how a phone feels to use. Extremely fast charging numbers and 200 MP zoom claims are mostly marketing.
Instead, read independent tests of battery life, update history and camera consistency, and check the IP rating: IP68 means the phone survives dust and a drop in the sink or pool.

Also think about repair. Check whether official spare batteries and screens are available, and how much a battery swap costs. Under EU rules, new phones must be designed so the battery lasts at least 800 full charge cycles while keeping 80% of its capacity.

8 GB RAM minimum, 12 GB for long-term use
256 GB storage if you record video
OLED, 120 Hz, 1,500+ nits peak brightness
Optical telephoto (3× or more) if photos matter
IP68 dust and water protection
Wireless charging and an 80% charge limit
Comfortable size and weight in your hand

Ignoring how many years of updates the model gets
Choosing 128 GB and running out of space in a year

faq.q: How long should a smartphone last in 2026?
faq.a: A well-chosen phone should last 5–7 years. The limit is usually software support and battery wear, not speed. Pick a model with a long update policy and replace the battery once if needed.

faq.q: Is 8 GB of RAM enough for a phone?
faq.a: 8 GB is enough for everyday use today. If you plan to keep the phone for many years or use on-device AI features heavily, 12 GB gives more headroom.

faq.q: Do I need a flagship phone?
faq.a: Not for most people. Mid-range phones now have good screens, all-day batteries and long updates. Flagships mainly add better zoom cameras, faster charging and premium materials.

faq.q: Is eSIM worth having?
faq.a: Yes, especially if you travel. eSIM lets you add a local data plan without a physical card. Some newer phones have dropped the SIM tray entirely, so check your carrier supports eSIM before buying.

title: How to choose a laptop in 2026
lead: Choose a laptop by weight, battery life, screen and memory first. Raw processor speed matters less than most spec sheets suggest.

p: Split laptops into three groups. Thin-and-light models (under 1.4 kg) are for students, office work and travel. All-rounders (1.4–1.9 kg, often 15–16 inches) suit home use and light creative work. Gaming and workstation laptops (2–3 kg) have a dedicated graphics card and are built for heavy loads, not for carrying every day.

Also decide on the operating system. Windows offers the widest choice, macOS gives long battery life and strong resale value, and ChromeOS is fine for browser-based work at the lowest prices. Windows 10 lost support in October 2025, so do not buy a used machine that cannot run Windows 11.

RAM is the most common bottleneck. 16 GB is the sensible minimum in 2026: browsers, video calls and on-device AI tools fill 8 GB quickly. Choose 32 GB for video editing, large spreadsheets, software development or gaming.
Many thin laptops have soldered memory that cannot be upgraded later, so buy enough now. For storage, pick an NVMe SSD of at least 512 GB. 1 TB is worth it if you keep photos or games locally.

Current mid-range chips from all major makers handle office work, streaming and photo editing with ease. Higher tiers help with sustained work like video exports or code compilation. Arm-based Windows laptops now run most apps well, but check that any specialist software or games you rely on are supported.

Integrated graphics are enough for everything except modern 3D games and serious 3D or video work. For gaming at 1080p–1440p, look for a dedicated GPU with at least 8 GB of VRAM; 6 GB or less is already limiting in new titles.
"Copilot+ PC" and AI-PC labels mean a built-in NPU of 40 TOPS or more. It powers some Windows features but is not a reason to pay much more on its own.

Ignore the maker's maximum battery figure; it is measured at low brightness doing light tasks. Look at independent tests of web browsing or video playback. 12 hours or more in such tests means a real full workday.

Battery capacity of 60–75 Wh is typical for thin laptops. Gaming laptops often have 80–99 Wh (the legal flight limit is 100 Wh) but still last only a few hours because of their power-hungry parts. Charging over USB-C is a big convenience.

You look at the screen all day. Look for at least 1920 × 1200 on 13–14 inch models and around 2.5K on 15–16 inch ones, plus 300+ nits brightness and good sRGB coverage (95–100%). OLED gives deep blacks; a matte IPS panel handles reflections better.
Test the keyboard and touchpad if you can. Check ports: at least two USB-C ports (ideally USB4 or Thunderbolt), one USB-A, and HDMI if you present often. Wi-Fi 6E or 7 is a nice bonus.

A laptop lives in a bag and on your lap, so build quality matters. Aluminium or magnesium chassis flex less than cheap plastic, and hinges that open with one hand are a good sign of careful engineering.

Fan noise is easy to overlook in a shop and hard to ignore at home. Thin laptops with powerful chips can get loud under load. Reviews that measure noise in decibels are useful: under 35 dB is quiet, over 45 dB is clearly audible in a silent room.
Finally, check repairability. A replaceable SSD, accessible battery and available spare parts can add years to a laptop's life and make it easier to resell.

Ignore high CPU clock speeds in GHz, core counts as a selling point, and "up to" battery claims. A 4K screen on a 14-inch laptop mostly drains the battery. Gaming laptops with flashy RGB lighting but weak cooling throttle under load.
Instead check sustained performance in reviews, fan noise, build quality and how easily the SSD can be replaced.

512 GB NVMe SSD or more
12+ hours in independent battery tests
1920 × 1200 or higher, 300+ nits
At least two USB-C ports with charging
Weight under 1.4 kg if you carry it daily
Dedicated GPU with 8 GB VRAM for gaming
Keyboard and touchpad tested in person
mistakes: Buying 8 GB of RAM in a laptop that cannot be upgraded
Trusting the maker's maximum battery figure
Choosing a gaming laptop for daily commuting
Paying for an AI label instead of more memory or a better screen

faq.q: Is 8 GB of RAM enough for a laptop in 2026?
faq.a: Only for very light use like browsing and documents. With modern browsers and Windows 11, 16 GB gives a much smoother experience and keeps the laptop usable for longer.

faq.q: Do I need a Copilot+ or AI PC?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The NPU powers some Windows AI features and better battery life in video calls, but most AI tools you use today run in the cloud. Memory and screen quality matter more.

faq.q: Should I choose an Arm or an x86 laptop?
faq.a: Arm laptops usually offer longer battery life and run most mainstream apps well. If you rely on older specialist software, some games with anti-cheat, or certain drivers, x86 is still the safer choice.

faq.q: How long does a laptop last?
faq.a: A good laptop lasts 5–7 years with enough RAM and storage. The battery may need replacing after 3–4 years, so models with easy battery and SSD access age better.

title: How to choose a tablet in 2026
lead: A tablet should match how you use it: media on the sofa, notes with a stylus or work with a keyboard. Screen, updates and accessories matter most.

p: Most tablets are used for video, reading and browsing. For that, any current mid-range model with a good screen is enough. If you want to take handwritten notes, draw or replace a laptop, you need stylus and keyboard support, more memory and a stronger chip.

Next, choose the platform. iPadOS has the biggest selection of tablet-optimised apps. Android tablets offer more choice in size and price, and some include memory card slots. Check which apps you rely on before switching.

8–9 inch tablets are light (around 300 g) and good for reading in one hand. 10–11 inches is the all-round size. 12–13 inch tablets are excellent for split-screen work and drawing, but weigh 550–700 g and are tiring to hold for long.

Look for at least 2,000 pixels on the long side, a 90–120 Hz refresh rate for smooth scrolling, and 500+ nits brightness. OLED and Mini-LED panels give much better contrast for films. A matte or anti-reflective coating helps if you read outdoors.

For streaming and browsing, any recent mid-range chip works. For drawing apps, video editing or many open apps, choose a top-tier chip. 8 GB of RAM is a good target in 2026; 4 GB already causes apps to reload.
Choose at least 128 GB of storage. Downloaded films and games fill 64 GB fast. If the tablet has a microSD slot, you can start smaller and add a card later.

If you plan to use desktop-style multitasking, such as several windows or an external monitor, check that the model supports it. On some platforms these features need a minimum amount of RAM or a top-tier chip.
Tablets are kept longer than phones, so updates matter. Check the official policy: good manufacturers now promise 5–7 years of OS and security updates. Cheap no-name tablets often get none at all.
Long support also keeps banking and streaming apps working, as they drop old OS versions over time.
Stylus and keyboard covers are often sold separately and can add a lot to the total cost. Make sure the stylus works with your exact model and generation; compatibility changes frequently.
A USB-C port with fast data transfer is useful for external drives and monitors. Cellular (5G) models cost more but save you from relying on phone hotspots. Wi-Fi 6 or newer is enough for most homes.
Also check charging. Many tablets ship without a charger, and a 20–45 W USB-C adapter makes a large difference to charging time compared with an old phone charger.

If you mainly read books, a 7–8 inch tablet or a dedicated e-reader may be more comfortable than a full-size tablet. E-ink screens are easier on the eyes for long reading and last weeks on a charge, but are poor for video and colour content.

For children, look for a sturdy case, good parental controls and a long update policy, since the tablet may be handed down. Multi-user profiles on some Android tablets make a shared family tablet easier to manage.
If the tablet will mostly stay at home on a stand, a larger screen and good speakers matter more than weight. Four-speaker setups make films and video calls much clearer without headphones.

Camera megapixels on a tablet barely matter; you mainly need a decent front camera for video calls, ideally placed on the long edge. Battery capacity in mAh is not comparable across platforms, so look at tested video playback hours instead (10+ hours is good).
Be careful with "laptop replacement" marketing. Check that your work apps, file management and external monitor support really meet your needs.
Also be wary of very cheap tablets with unknown chipsets. Slow storage and low memory make even simple apps feel sluggish, and they rarely receive security updates.

90–120 Hz and 500+ nits
8 GB RAM for multitasking or drawing
128 GB storage or a microSD slot
5+ years of promised updates
Stylus and keyboard compatibility confirmed
Front camera on the long edge for video calls
10+ hours in independent video tests

Forgetting the cost of the stylus and keyboard
Choosing a cheap tablet with no update policy
Buying a 13-inch tablet mostly for reading in bed

faq.q: Can a tablet replace a laptop?
faq.a: For browsing, email, documents and video calls, often yes with a keyboard cover. For complex office work, coding or specialist software, a laptop is still more practical.

faq.q: What size tablet is best?
faq.a: 10–11 inches is the best all-round size. Choose 8–9 inches for reading and portability, and 12–13 inches for drawing, split-screen work or a laptop-like experience.

faq.q: Do I need a cellular tablet?
faq.a: Only if you often use it away from Wi-Fi, for example while commuting or travelling. Otherwise a phone hotspot is usually enough and the Wi-Fi model is cheaper.

faq.q: How much storage does a tablet need?
faq.a: 128 GB suits most people. Choose 256 GB or more if you download lots of films, play large games or work with video, unless the tablet accepts a microSD card.

title: How to choose a TV in 2026
lead: Pick the TV size from your seating distance, then the panel type for your room's light. Processing, HDR and gaming ports come next.

p: Think about the room and how you watch. A bright living room with daytime viewing needs a different TV than a dark home cinema. Films, sport and gaming each put different demands on the screen.

Size is the decision people regret most, and almost always because they bought too small. For 4K, a good rule is a screen diagonal of about 0.6–0.7 times your viewing distance. At 2.5 m from the sofa, that means 60–70 inches; at 2 m, around 55 inches.
OLED and QD-OLED have perfect blacks and wide viewing angles. They are the best choice for films in dim rooms. Modern OLEDs are brighter than before, but very bright rooms still favour LCD.

Mini-LED LCD TVs use thousands of small backlight LEDs in local dimming zones. They reach 1,500–3,000 nits or more, so HDR looks punchy even in daylight. More dimming zones means less blooming around bright objects.

Basic edge-lit LCD or direct-lit TVs without local dimming are fine for casual viewing but show greyish blacks in a dark room. VA panels give better contrast than IPS, while IPS keeps colours when watched from the side.
4K is standard on every TV of 43 inches and up. 8K offers no visible benefit at normal viewing distances, and there is almost no 8K content.

For HDR, real peak brightness matters more than logos. Aim for 600+ nits for visible HDR effect; 1,000+ nits is where it gets impressive. Dolby Vision and HDR10+ are both used by streaming services; having both is a bonus, not a must.
Processing quality matters too. A good processor upscales HD broadcasts and streams cleanly and handles fast motion in sport without blur. Independent reviews test this better than any spec sheet.

For a current console or gaming PC, look for a native 120 Hz panel (or 144 Hz and above for PC), HDMI 2.1 on at least two ports, VRR and ALLM. Some TVs only have HDMI 2.1 on one or two of four ports, so check carefully if you have several devices.
If you use a soundbar, eARC lets it play lossless and Dolby Atmos audio from the TV's apps. Count the HDMI ports you need today and add one spare.
Input lag matters for gaming too. In game mode, good TVs reach under 10–15 ms, which feels instant. Reviews measure this; marketing material rarely mentions it.

Built-in speakers on thin TVs are weak. Plan for a soundbar if dialogue clarity matters to you. The smart platform decides which apps you get and for how long; check that all your streaming services are supported and that the brand has a track record of updates.
Compare the EU energy label and the typical power use in watts. A 65-inch TV can use anywhere from about 80 W to over 200 W in normal SDR mode, which adds up over years of daily viewing.
Measure the wall or TV unit before you buy. A 65-inch TV is about 145 cm wide, and a 75-inch model about 167 cm. Check where the feet sit: many TVs have feet near the edges, which need a wide stand.
For wall mounting, note the VESA pattern and weight, and ideally mount the screen so its centre is near eye level when you sit. Mounting it high above a fireplace often causes neck strain.

After setup, switch off motion smoothing for films, choose the most accurate picture mode, and turn on energy-saving features you are happy with. These few minutes make a bigger difference than most upgrades.
"Motion rate 240" and similar numbers are processing tricks, not the real refresh rate. Contrast ratios such as "1,000,000:1" are not comparable between brands. AI picture modes often oversharpen.
Showroom demos use vivid modes under bright lights. At home, use Filmmaker or Cinema mode for the most accurate picture.

Also compare the real panel, not just the model name. Some ranges use different panel types in different sizes, so a 55-inch and a 65-inch model from the same series can perform differently. Reviews of your exact size are the safest guide.

600+ nits real HDR brightness
Native 120 Hz panel for gaming
HDMI 2.1 on all ports you need
eARC if you use a soundbar

faq.q: What size TV should I buy?
faq.a: Multiply your viewing distance by about 0.6–0.7 to get the ideal 4K screen size. At 2.5 m that is 60–70 inches. Most people who upgrade say they wish they had gone bigger.

faq.q: Is OLED or Mini-LED better?
faq.a: OLED has perfect blacks and is best for films in dim rooms. Mini-LED gets brighter and suits daytime viewing in bright rooms. Both are excellent at the high end.

faq.q: Do I need HDMI 2.1?
faq.a: Only for gaming at 4K and 120 Hz on a current console or PC. For streaming, broadcast TV and Blu-ray, HDMI 2.0 is enough.

faq.q: Is 8K worth it in 2026?
faq.a: No for almost everyone. There is very little 8K content and at normal viewing distances you cannot see the difference from 4K. A better 4K panel gives more for the money.

title: How to choose a monitor in 2026
lead: Match resolution to screen size, refresh rate to your use, and panel type to your room. Ports and ergonomics decide daily comfort.

p: Office work, creative work and gaming need different monitors. Office users want sharp text and good ergonomics. Photo and video editors need accurate colour. Gamers want high refresh rates and fast response.
Also check your desk depth. At 60–80 cm viewing distance, 27 inches is the comfortable sweet spot. 32 inches works on deeper desks, and 34-inch ultrawides need at least 70 cm of depth.
Pixel density decides how sharp text looks. Good pairings: 24 inches at 1920 × 1080, 27 inches at 2560 × 1440 or 3840 × 2160, 32 inches at 3840 × 2160. A 27-inch Full HD monitor looks soft for text.
4K on 27 inches is very sharp but needs scaling and a stronger graphics card for gaming. 1440p on 27 inches is the best balance for most gamers.

Check your operating system scaling too. On Windows, 27-inch 4K usually runs at 150% scaling, which looks crisp. On macOS, 27-inch 4K works, but 5K at the same size gives the sharpest text without compromises.

For office work, 60–100 Hz is fine, though 100–120 Hz makes scrolling noticeably smoother. For gaming, 144–180 Hz is the mainstream target; 240 Hz and higher helps competitive shooters if your PC can reach those frame rates.

Response time claims of 1 ms are measured in best-case modes. Read independent tests for real motion clarity. OLED monitors respond almost instantly, while fast IPS panels are close behind. Adaptive sync (FreeSync or G-SYNC compatible) removes tearing and is essential for gaming.

IPS panels give accurate colours and wide viewing angles. VA panels offer 2–3 times higher contrast, which suits dark rooms and films. OLED and QD-OLED combine perfect blacks with fast response, but can suffer burn-in from static elements over years; check the warranty terms.

For photo editing, look for 99–100% sRGB coverage and, for video or HDR work, 90%+ DCI-P3. For real HDR, look for DisplayHDR 600 or higher, or DisplayHDR True Black on OLED. DisplayHDR 400 gives little visible benefit.
Factory calibration reports and a dedicated sRGB mode are helpful if you edit photos for the web, because wide-gamut monitors can make normal content look oversaturated without one.
A USB-C port with 65–90 W power delivery can charge a laptop and carry video over one cable, which is ideal for home offices. A built-in USB hub or KVM switch helps if you use two computers.

A stand with height, tilt and swivel adjustment protects your neck. If the stand is basic, check for a VESA 100 × 100 mount so you can use a monitor arm. For gaming at high refresh rates, make sure you have DisplayPort 1.4 or 2.1, or HDMI 2.1.

If you spend many hours in front of the screen, look for flicker-free backlighting and a low blue light mode. A matte coating reduces reflections from windows and lamps; glossy screens look punchier but need careful placement.

Two 24 or 27-inch monitors give flexible space for multitasking. A single 34-inch ultrawide with 3440 × 1440 resolution offers similar space without a gap in the middle, and suits video editing timelines and racing games.
Check the energy label and typical power use as well. Large, bright monitors and especially high-refresh models can draw 40–80 W, which matters if the screen is on all day.
Dynamic contrast ratios, "HDR-ready" labels without certification, and gaming modes that oversharpen are mostly marketing. Built-in speakers are usually weak.
A curved screen matters only for ultrawide and very large monitors. On 24–27 inch models it adds little.

100 Hz+ for office, 144 Hz+ for gaming
Adaptive sync for gaming
99–100% sRGB for photo work
DisplayHDR 600+ if HDR matters
USB-C with laptop charging for home office
Height-adjustable stand or VESA mount
Correct DisplayPort or HDMI version for your GPU

Trusting 1 ms response time claims
Paying for 240 Hz when the PC cannot reach those frame rates

faq.q: Is 1440p or 4K better for a 27-inch monitor?
faq.a: 4K is sharper for text and photo work. 1440p is the better choice for gaming because it is easier to drive at high frame rates. Both are good; 1080p on 27 inches is not.

faq.q: Do I need 144 Hz for office work?
faq.a: No. 60 Hz works, but 100–120 Hz makes scrolling and mouse movement feel smoother. Many affordable office monitors now offer 100 Hz.

faq.q: Is OLED burn-in still a problem?
faq.a: Modern OLED monitors have protection features and many come with burn-in warranties. Risk remains with static content like taskbars displayed many hours a day, so check warranty terms if you work on one all day.

faq.q: What is USB-C power delivery on a monitor?
faq.a: It lets one cable carry video, data and charging power to a laptop. Look for 65 W or more for most laptops, and 90 W or more for larger models.

title: How to choose headphones in 2026
lead: Choose the form factor first, then noise cancelling, comfort and battery life. Codecs and driver sizes matter far less than fit.

p: Decide where you will use them. In-ear earbuds are small and good for commuting and sport. Over-ear headphones are more comfortable for long sessions, flights and offices, and usually sound fuller. Open-ear designs keep you aware of traffic, which is useful for running and cycling.
Also check your phone. Some features, such as spatial audio, high-quality codecs and fast pairing, work best within one brand's ecosystem.

Comfort decides whether you actually wear them. For earbuds, a secure seal matters for both bass and noise cancelling; try all ear tip sizes. For over-ear models, weight under 300 g and soft, deep ear cushions help over hours.
If you wear glasses, check how the cushions seal around the frames. Some models also offer replaceable cushions and batteries, which extends their life.
Sound leakage matters in quiet offices and libraries. Closed-back designs keep your music private, while open-back headphones sound more spacious but let sound out and in.

Active noise cancelling (ANC) is the main reason to pay more. The best models remove most engine and train rumble, while cheaper ANC mainly reduces low hum. Read independent measurements rather than claims like "-50 dB".
A good transparency mode lets you hear announcements and talk without removing the headphones. Adaptive ANC that adjusts automatically is convenient in changing environments.
Wind noise reduction is another useful feature for cyclists and people who walk a lot outdoors, as some ANC systems make a loud rumbling sound in windy conditions.

For earbuds, aim for 6+ hours per charge with ANC on, plus 20–30 hours from the case. For over-ear headphones, 30 hours or more with ANC is now common. Fast charging (10 minutes for several hours) is useful.
Multipoint lets you stay connected to a phone and laptop at once, which is valuable for work. Bluetooth 5.3 or newer with LE Audio support prepares you for Auracast broadcast audio in public spaces.
Check whether the headphones can be used with a cable when the battery runs out. A USB-C or 3.5 mm wired mode is useful on flights and for gaming.

Most people prefer a balanced sound with a slight bass lift. An app with an equaliser lets you adjust it. Codecs such as LDAC or aptX Adaptive can carry more data, but only if your phone supports them; iPhones use AAC.
For video and gaming, check latency. Low-latency modes help lip sync, but for competitive gaming a wired or 2.4 GHz dongle connection is still better.

If you take calls on your headphones, microphone quality matters as much as sound. Look for reviews that test calls in windy streets and noisy cafes. Models with several beam-forming microphones and bone-conduction sensors pick up your voice more clearly.

For office work, a headset with a boom microphone or certification for business video platforms gives the clearest voice. Earbuds with stems usually perform better on calls than round, stemless designs.
Also check how the headphones handle switching between devices and whether a mute button or touch control is easy to find without looking.

Driver size in mm and frequency ranges like "5 Hz – 40 kHz" say little about real sound quality. "Hi-Res" logos on Bluetooth headphones depend on the codec chain. Impedance only matters for wired headphones on weak sources; above about 80 Ω you may need an amplifier.
Check the IP rating for sport: IPX4 handles sweat and rain, while IP55 or higher adds dust protection.
Instead, look at measured frequency response graphs and independent listening tests, which show far more than marketing numbers.

Comfortable fit tested with all tip sizes
Strong ANC and a natural transparency mode
6+ h (earbuds) or 30+ h (over-ear) with ANC
Multipoint for phone and laptop
Codec your phone actually supports
IPX4 or better for sport
App with equaliser and firmware updates

Paying for LDAC or aptX when the phone does not support it
Ignoring comfort for long listening sessions
Using Bluetooth earbuds for competitive gaming

faq.q: Are over-ear or in-ear headphones better?
faq.a: Over-ear headphones are usually more comfortable for long sessions and cancel noise better on flights. Earbuds are more portable and better for sport and commuting. Many people own one of each.

faq.q: Is noise cancelling bad for your ears?
faq.a: No. ANC actually lets you listen at lower volume in noisy places, which is better for your hearing. Some people feel slight pressure at first; most get used to it.

faq.q: Which Bluetooth codec is best?
faq.a: It depends on your phone. Android phones often support LDAC or aptX Adaptive, while iPhones use AAC. With good headphones, the difference between codecs is small for most listeners.

faq.q: How long do wireless earbuds last?
faq.a: Usually 2–4 years, limited by the small batteries. Models with replaceable batteries or good repair programmes last longer.

title: How to choose a smartwatch in 2026
lead: Compatibility with your phone, battery life and the health and sport features you will really use matter more than screen size or app counts.

p: Check phone compatibility first. Some watches work only with one phone platform, and many features need the maker's own app. A watch that does not fully support your phone is a poor buy at any price.

Then decide what you want: notifications and payments, fitness and running, or detailed health tracking. Full smartwatches do all three but need charging every 1–3 days. Fitness-focused watches and hybrid watches do fewer apps but last 1–3 weeks.
If you only want step counting, sleep tracking and notifications, a fitness band may be enough. Bands are lighter, cheaper and last a week or more on a charge.

Battery life is the most common complaint. Full smartwatches with always-on screens usually last 1–2 days; newer models reach 2–3 days. Sport watches from fitness brands often last 7–20 days, even with an AMOLED screen.

Look at tested battery life with your settings: always-on display, GPS workouts and sleep tracking all use power. If you want sleep tracking, you need a watch that easily lasts the night and charges quickly in the morning.
Charging speed helps too. Some watches charge from 0 to 80% in about 30–45 minutes, so a short charge during a shower is enough for the day.

Case sizes run from about 38 mm to 49 mm. Measure your wrist; on wrists under 16 cm, cases above 44 mm often look and feel large. Lighter watches (under 40 g without strap) are more comfortable for sleep.
An AMOLED screen with always-on mode and 1,000+ nits peak brightness stays readable outdoors. Sapphire glass and titanium cases resist scratches better than standard glass and aluminium.
All smartwatches track heart rate with an optical sensor, but accuracy varies, especially in intense intervals. If you train seriously, check independent sensor tests or plan to pair a chest strap.

For running, hiking and cycling, dual-band (L1 + L5) GPS gives clearly more accurate tracks near tall buildings and trees. ECG, blood oxygen (SpO2), skin temperature and irregular rhythm alerts are useful screening tools, but they are not a medical diagnosis. Fall detection and crash detection are valuable for older users and solo outdoor sports.

If you have a medical condition, ask your doctor which features are approved in your country. Some functions such as ECG or blood pressure alerts are cleared only in certain regions and may be switched off elsewhere.
NFC lets you pay with the watch; check that your bank supports the watch's payment system. LTE models can call and stream without your phone, but need a separate mobile plan and use more battery.
Water resistance of 5 ATM covers swimming in a pool. For diving or water sports, look for 10 ATM or more, or a dive certification.
Some brands put advanced health insights, training plans or detailed sleep analysis behind a monthly subscription. Check what works for free and what costs extra before comparing prices.

Software support matters too. Good makers update watches for 3–5 years with new features and security fixes, while cheap brands may stop after a year. A longer update policy also keeps the companion app compatible with your next phone.
If you want to change straps, check the strap width and mechanism. Standard 20 mm or 22 mm quick-release pins let you use cheap third-party straps; proprietary systems limit your choice.
App store size matters less than you think; most people use a handful of apps. Stress, energy and readiness scores are estimates, not measurements, and differ widely between brands.
Also check software support and repair: how long the maker updates the watch, and whether the battery can be replaced.

faq.q: Can I use a smartwatch with any phone?
faq.a: No. Some watches work only with one phone platform, and others lose features with the wrong phone. Always check compatibility before buying.

faq.q: How accurate are smartwatch health sensors?
faq.a: Heart rate at rest and steps are usually accurate. Readings during intense exercise, blood oxygen and sleep stages are less precise. Use them as trends, not diagnoses.

faq.q: Do I need an LTE smartwatch?
faq.a: Only if you want to leave your phone at home, for example on runs. LTE needs a separate plan with your carrier and reduces battery life.

faq.q: Can I swim with a smartwatch?
faq.a: Most watches rated 5 ATM or more are safe for pool and sea swimming. They are not built for high-pressure water like jet skiing or diving unless rated for it.

title: How to choose a speaker in 2026
lead: Decide between portable Bluetooth and home Wi-Fi speakers first. Then size the speaker to your space and check battery, durability and streaming support.

p: Portable Bluetooth speakers are for the beach, garden, shower or travel. They run on batteries and connect directly to your phone. Home Wi-Fi speakers stay plugged in, stream from services directly, support multiroom playback and often include a voice assistant.
Some speakers do both, with Wi-Fi at home and Bluetooth outdoors. They cost more and weigh more, so only pay for it if you will use both modes.

Think about who controls the music. At parties, speakers that let several phones join and take turns are practical. For a home office, a small speaker with a built-in microphone can double as a conference speakerphone.

sections.h: Size and power for your space
p: Small speakers under 500 g are fine for personal listening, a desk or a hotel room. For a 20 m² room or a small garden gathering, look for medium speakers of 1–2 kg with 20–40 W of real (RMS) power. For larger parties outdoors, you need bigger party speakers of 4 kg and more.
Physics still applies: real bass needs larger drivers and cabinet volume. Tiny speakers with "deep bass" claims mostly use processing that reduces bass at higher volume.

A pair of speakers in stereo, or a single speaker with separate woofer and tweeters, gives clearer sound than a single full-range driver. Many brands let you pair two identical speakers for stereo, which is often better value than one larger speaker.
A companion app with an equaliser helps adjust bass and treble. For home speakers, room correction that tunes the sound to your room makes a noticeable difference.

Listen at the volume you normally use. Some speakers sound great quietly but distort when pushed, while others only come alive when loud. Reviews that test at several volume levels are the most useful.

For portable speakers, 12+ hours of real playback is good; tests at moderate volume are more useful than maximum claims, as loud playback can halve battery life. USB-C charging is standard; some speakers can also charge your phone.

Check the IP rating. IP67 means the speaker is dustproof and survives immersion in 1 m of water for 30 minutes; IPX4 only handles splashes. A rugged build and floating design help at the pool or beach.

Replaceable batteries are rare but extend a speaker's life considerably. Under EU rules, more portable devices will need user-replaceable batteries in the coming years, so check the maker's battery service options.

Bluetooth 5.3 or newer gives stable range. Codec support matters less on speakers than on headphones. For home speakers, check support for your streaming services, AirPlay 2 or Google Cast, and whether they work in a multiroom system with speakers you already own.
If you plan to use them with a TV, check for HDMI eARC or optical input; otherwise Bluetooth may cause lip-sync delay.

For music at home, a pair of passive bookshelf speakers with a small amplifier often sounds better than a single smart speaker at a similar price. Smart speakers win on convenience, voice control and multiroom.

For TV sound, a soundbar is usually a better choice than a Bluetooth speaker. Look for a dedicated centre channel for clear dialogue, HDMI eARC, and a separate subwoofer if you want strong bass in a room larger than 20 m².
Place speakers away from corners to avoid boomy bass, and at roughly ear height when you sit. Simple positioning changes often improve sound more than spending more money.
Peak power or "PMPO" watts are inflated numbers; use RMS power if it is listed. Wide frequency ranges on small speakers rarely reflect audible bass. Party light shows look fun but use battery.
Voice assistants are only useful if you will actually use them; some people prefer models with a physical microphone switch.

faq.q: How many watts does a speaker need?
faq.a: For personal listening, 5–10 W RMS is enough. For a living room of about 20 m², 20–40 W RMS works well. Large outdoor parties need 100 W or more.

faq.q: Is a Bluetooth or Wi-Fi speaker better?
faq.a: Bluetooth is simpler and portable. Wi-Fi offers better sound quality, multiroom and streaming without draining your phone. For home use, Wi-Fi is usually the better choice.

faq.q: Can I pair two speakers for stereo?
faq.a: Many models support stereo pairing, but usually only with an identical model or the same brand. Check this feature before buying a second unit.

faq.q: What does IP67 mean for a speaker?
faq.a: IP67 means fully dustproof and able to survive immersion in 1 m of water for 30 minutes. It is the right level for beaches, pools and hiking.

title: How to choose a camera in 2026
lead: A dedicated camera only beats a phone with a bigger sensor and better lenses. Choose sensor size, system and handling before megapixels.

p: Phones handle snapshots well. A separate camera makes sense for sports and wildlife (fast autofocus and long lenses), portraits with real background blur, low-light events, and serious video work.

Decide on the type. Mirrorless cameras with interchangeable lenses are the main choice in 2026; new DSLR models have largely stopped. Compact cameras with a fixed lens are smaller and simpler. Action cameras are for sport and rough conditions.

Be honest about how much you will carry it. A small camera you take everywhere beats a large one that stays in a cupboard. Many photographers end up with a compact for travel and a larger kit for planned shoots.

Sensor size has the biggest effect on image quality. A 1-inch sensor is clearly larger than most phone main sensors, although a few flagship phones now use one too. APS-C is about 3 times larger than 1-inch, and full frame is about 2.3 times larger than APS-C.

Larger sensors mean cleaner images in low light and stronger background blur, but also bigger, heavier and more expensive lenses. APS-C is the best balance for most enthusiasts; full frame suits low-light, portrait and professional work; Micro Four Thirds is compact and strong for video.
You buy into a lens system, not just a camera body. Check the range and price of lenses for the mount, including third-party options. A good lens often matters more than a newer body.
Kit lenses are fine to start. A fast prime lens, such as 50 mm f/1.8 on full frame or a similar equivalent, is an affordable step up for portraits and low light.
Zoom lenses with a constant f/2.8 or f/4 aperture are versatile for events and travel, but large and costly. Lighter variable-aperture zooms such as f/3.5–5.6 are good enough in daylight.
Modern subject-detection autofocus tracks eyes of people, animals, birds and vehicles. For sports and wildlife, look at burst speed (10–20+ frames per second) and buffer depth in reviews.

In-body image stabilisation (IBIS) gives sharp handheld shots at slower shutter speeds and smoother video with any lens. An electronic viewfinder helps in bright sun; a flip-out screen helps for vlogging and low angles. Hold the camera before buying; grip and controls decide daily comfort.

4K at 30 fps is standard. For smooth slow motion, look for 4K at 60 or 120 fps. 10-bit recording and Log profiles give more room for colour grading. Check recording limits and overheating in reviews, plus microphone and headphone jacks for serious video.

For vlogging, also look for a good front-facing screen, a wide lens around 16–20 mm equivalent, and digital stabilisation that works while walking. Continuous recording beyond 30 minutes and USB-C power during recording are useful for long events and streaming.
The camera body is only part of the cost. Plan for a spare battery, a fast memory card (UHS-II or CFexpress for high-end video and burst shooting), a bag and possibly a second lens.
Buying a body from the previous generation or a used lens from a reputable dealer is often the best value. Camera bodies change slowly, and good lenses hold their value for many years.

Weight also counts. A full-frame body with a large zoom can weigh 1.5–2 kg. If you travel or hike, a lighter APS-C or Micro Four Thirds kit that you actually carry will take more photos than a heavy one left at home.

More megapixels are not always better. 24–33 MP is plenty for most people; 45–60 MP is useful for landscapes and heavy cropping but needs sharper lenses and more storage. Maximum ISO values such as 102,400 are rarely usable.
Digital zoom figures on compacts are also misleading; only optical zoom counts.

faq.q: Is a camera better than a smartphone in 2026?
faq.a: Yes, when you need a bigger sensor, real zoom lenses or fast autofocus for action. For casual snapshots in good light, a modern phone is often enough.

faq.q: APS-C or full frame?
faq.a: APS-C is lighter and cheaper, with excellent quality for most people. Full frame is better in low light and for shallow depth of field, but the lenses cost and weigh more.

faq.q: How many megapixels do I need?
faq.a: 24 MP is enough for large prints and most uses. Higher resolution helps with cropping and landscapes, but files are larger and need sharper lenses.

faq.q: Are DSLRs still worth buying?
faq.a: Used DSLRs can be good value, but most new development is now in mirrorless systems. For a long-term investment in lenses, mirrorless is the safer choice.

title: How to choose a projector in 2026
lead: Brightness, room light and throw distance decide whether a projector looks great or washed out. Here is what to check before you buy.

p: Decide where the projector will live. A dark home cinema, a living room with windows and a portable setup for the garden are three different products. Room light matters more than any other factor: a projector that looks stunning at night can look grey at 4 pm.

Then measure. Note the distance from the projector position to the wall or screen, the screen width you want, and whether you can mount it on the ceiling or need it on a table. Also think about use: films, sport, gaming or office slides each favour different strengths.

sections.h: Brightness: ANSI lumens, not marketing lumens
p: Only trust brightness quoted in ANSI lumens or ISO 21118 lumens. Many cheap projectors advertise "LED lumens" or "light source lumens", which can be five to ten times higher than what reaches the screen.

As a rough guide: 1,000–1,500 ANSI lumens is enough for a fully dark room and a 100-inch (2.5 m diagonal) image. A living room with dimmed lights needs 2,000–3,000. For daytime viewing with some daylight, look for 3,000 or more, and accept that contrast will still suffer. Bigger screens need more light: doubling the width needs about four times the brightness for the same result.

1080p is still fine for screens under about 100 inches viewed from 3 m or more. For larger images or closer seating, 4K is worth it. Most affordable "4K" projectors use pixel shifting: the chip is 1080p or 2716 × 1528 and moves the image quickly to show 3840 × 2160 positions. It looks sharper than 1080p, but not quite as crisp as a native 4K panel.

Contrast decides how deep blacks look in a dark room. Ignore "dynamic contrast" figures of 1,000,000:1 or more; native contrast is the honest number, and few brands publish it. Reviews with measured contrast are the safest guide. HDR support helps only if the projector is bright enough, roughly 2,000 ANSI lumens or more.

Throw ratio tells you how far back the projector must sit. Distance = throw ratio × image width. With a ratio of 1.2, a 2.2 m wide image (about 100 inches) needs about 2.65 m. Short-throw models (0.4–0.8) work from 1–1.8 m. Ultra-short-throw units (below 0.4) sit just centimetres from the wall, but need a very flat wall or a special light-rejecting screen.

Optical zoom and lens shift let you place the projector off-centre without distorting the picture. Digital keystone correction also fixes the shape, but it scales the image and reduces sharpness. If placement is fixed, prefer optical adjustment.

Laser and LED light sources last 20,000–30,000 hours, start instantly and keep their brightness longer. Classic lamps cost less up front but last 3,000–6,000 hours (more in eco mode) and dim over time, so budget for replacement lamps.

Fan noise matters in a quiet room. Below about 30 dB is barely noticeable; above 35 dB you will hear it in quiet scenes. For gaming, look for input lag under 20 ms in game mode and HDMI 2.1 if you want 4K at higher frame rates. Single-chip DLP projectors with a colour wheel can show brief "rainbow" flashes to sensitive viewers; RGB laser and LCD/LCoS designs avoid this.
Check the inputs too. Two HDMI ports are useful if you connect a console and a streaming box, and an eARC output lets you send sound to a soundbar or receiver.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Be sceptical of very cheap projectors promising 4K, 10,000+ lumens and "1080p native" in the same listing. Often the panel is lower resolution and the lumen figure is not ANSI. Built-in speakers are rarely good; plan for a soundbar or speakers. Smart TV apps are convenient but often limited by streaming licences, so a separate streaming stick may work better.

At least 2,000 ANSI lumens if the room is not fully dark

faq.q: How many lumens do I need for a living room?
faq.a: For a living room with some ambient light, aim for 2,000–3,000 ANSI lumens. If you watch in daylight, go higher and consider an ambient-light-rejecting screen. In a fully dark room, 1,000–1,500 ANSI lumens is enough.

faq.q: Is a projector better than a TV?
faq.a: A projector gives a much larger image for the money, often 100–120 inches. A TV is brighter, has better contrast in daylight and needs no screen or careful placement. Many people use a projector for films at night and a TV for daily viewing.

faq.q: Is pixel-shifting 4K real 4K?
faq.a: It shows a 3840 × 2160 signal by moving a lower-resolution image very quickly. It is clearly sharper than 1080p, but slightly softer than a native 4K panel. For most viewers at normal distances the difference is small.

faq.q: Can I project onto a white wall?
faq.a: Yes, a smooth, matte white or light grey wall works well in a dark room. A proper screen improves uniformity and contrast. Ultra-short-throw projectors show every wall bump, so a flat screen is strongly recommended for them.

title: How to choose a graphics card in 2026
lead: Match the graphics card to your monitor, your games and your power supply. Video memory, upscaling support and physical fit matter more than headline specs.

p: Your monitor sets the target. For 1080p at 60–144 Hz, a mid-range card is plenty. For 1440p at 144 Hz or more, you need an upper mid-range card. 4K at high settings with ray tracing still requires a high-end card, even with upscaling.

Also look at the rest of your PC. An older 4- or 6-core processor can hold back a fast card, especially at 1080p. Check your power supply wattage and connectors, and the free space in your case, before you choose. If you work with AI models, 3D rendering or video, video memory and software support may matter more than gaming speed.

VRAM holds textures and other game data. When it runs out, games stutter or force you to lower settings. In 2026, 8 GB is the bare minimum for 1080p and already limiting in some new titles. Aim for 12 GB for 1080p and entry 1440p, 16 GB for 1440p with high textures and ray tracing, and 16 GB or more for 4K. Local AI models benefit from as much VRAM as you can afford.

Memory bus width (128-bit, 192-bit, 256-bit) and memory type (GDDR6, GDDR7) affect bandwidth, but they only make sense when comparing cards of the same generation. Benchmarks tell you more than either number alone.

Compare cards using independent benchmarks at your resolution, not core counts or clock speeds. Shader core numbers cannot be compared across brands or generations. Look at average frame rates and 1% lows, which show stutter.

Upscaling (DLSS, FSR, XeSS) renders at lower resolution and rebuilds a sharper image. Recent versions look very close to native resolution and can add 30–70% more frames. Frame generation adds extra frames on top, but it does not reduce input lag, so it works best when you already have 50–60 fps. Ray tracing performance still varies a lot between brands, so check benchmarks for the games you play.

Check the recommended minimum power supply. Mid-range cards usually need a 550–650 W unit; high-end cards often ask for 750–1,000 W. Many current cards use a 12V-2x6 (16-pin) connector; make sure it is fully seated and avoid sharp cable bends near the plug.

Measure your case. Many cards are 300–340 mm long and take 2.5 to 3.5 slots. Also check the PCI Express link: some budget cards use only 8 lanes, which can cost performance on older PCIe 3.0 motherboards. Cooling with two or three large fans usually means lower noise.

Most cards have one HDMI and three DisplayPort outputs. For a 4K TV at 120 Hz you need HDMI 2.1; for very high refresh monitors, DisplayPort 2.1 gives more headroom. Video encoders (AV1 support is now standard) matter for streaming and screen recording. For creative apps and AI tools, check that your software supports the brand you choose.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Factory overclocks usually add only 2–5% performance; pay extra for a better cooler or quieter fans rather than higher clocks. RGB lighting adds cost, not speed. Be careful with model names: two cards with similar names can have different memory sizes or chip versions, so check the exact specs. Frame generation numbers in marketing charts are not comparable to normal frame rates.

Finally, think about lifespan. A card with more VRAM and support for the latest upscaling version usually stays useful for longer, because new games lean on both. Spending a little more for 16 GB instead of 8 GB is often the best upgrade you can make.

At least 12 GB VRAM for new games at 1080p–1440p

faq.q: How much VRAM do I need in 2026?
faq.a: Aim for 12 GB at 1080p and 1440p, and 16 GB or more for 4K or heavy ray tracing. 8 GB still runs many games, but new titles increasingly need lower texture settings on such cards.

faq.q: Will a new graphics card work in my old PC?
faq.a: Usually yes, since PCI Express is backward compatible. Check the power supply, the power connectors, the case space and whether your processor is fast enough not to hold the card back.

faq.q: Is frame generation worth using?
faq.a: It makes motion look smoother when you already have about 50–60 fps. It does not make the game respond faster, so competitive players often switch it off. In slower single-player games it can be a good upgrade.

faq.q: Should I buy a used graphics card?
faq.a: It can be good value if the seller can show it working and it has no damage or overheating. Check remaining warranty and avoid cards with modified firmware. Test it under load before you finalise the purchase if possible.

title: How to choose a game console in 2026
lead: The right console depends on the games you want, where you play and how much you will spend on games and subscriptions over the years.

p: Start with the games, not the hardware. Each platform has exclusive series, and friends you play with online matter too. Write down five games you want to play and check which systems have them.

Then decide where you play. A home console connects to your TV. A hybrid or handheld can be played on the go and on the TV. Handheld gaming PCs run PC game libraries but need more tinkering. Think about who plays: young children, a family sharing one device, or one player who wants the best graphics.

sections.h: Total cost, not just the box
p: The console price is only the start. Online multiplayer on most platforms requires a paid subscription, and game-library subscriptions add more. New games often cost more than the console accessories you budget for. A second controller, extra storage and a charging solution are common extras.

Digital-only editions save money at checkout but lock you out of used and borrowed discs. If you buy many games, a disc drive can pay for itself. Check family sharing and parental-control rules as well.

Big games now take 50–150 GB each, and the system software uses part of the drive. A console with about 1 TB of storage holds only a handful of large titles. Choose a model with expandable storage and check what type it takes: some use standard M.2 NVMe SSDs, others use proprietary expansion cards or specific microSD Express cards. Older, slower cards may not run current games.

To get 4K at 120 frames per second from a home console, your TV needs an HDMI 2.1 port that supports 4K 120 Hz. VRR (variable refresh rate) and ALLM (auto low latency mode) make games smoother and more responsive. Without them the console still works, just at 60 Hz.

For handhelds, look at the built-in screen: size around 7–8 inches, refresh rate of 120 Hz for smoother motion, and whether it is OLED or LCD. OLED gives deeper blacks and often better battery life with dark content.

Handheld battery life usually ranges from 2 to 8 hours. Demanding 3D games sit at the low end; simple or older games last longer. Check whether the device charges over USB-C with a standard charger, which makes travel easier. Weight matters too: anything over about 600 g gets tiring in long sessions.
If you travel, check whether the handheld supports offline play for your games and whether cloud saves sync between devices. A protective case and a screen protector are worth buying from day one.

Try the controller if you can. Grip size, button layout and trigger feel differ between platforms, and you will hold it for hundreds of hours. Spare controllers are expensive, so check the price before buying for a family. Rechargeable controllers with USB-C are easiest to live with.

All major platforms offer parental controls for play time, spending and online chat, usually managed from a phone app. Accessibility options such as button remapping, text size and adaptive controllers vary, so check them if anyone in your home needs them. Backward compatibility also matters: being able to play your existing games on a new console saves money.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Teraflops do not translate directly into better-looking games; developer support and the game library matter more. "8K" on the box means very little today. Pro or upgraded models offer better image quality and frame rates, but only if your TV can show the difference and the games are patched for it. Bundles are good value only if you want the included game.

faq.q: Do I need a 4K TV for a new console?
faq.a: No. All current consoles work with 1080p TVs and many games look better than before even at 1080p. A 4K TV with HDMI 2.1 lets you see the full image quality and high frame rates.

faq.q: Is a digital-only console a good idea?
faq.a: It is cheaper and smaller, and fine if you buy games on sale in the online store. You lose the ability to buy, sell or borrow discs. Over several years the disc version can work out cheaper for heavy players.

faq.q: Do I need an online subscription?
faq.a: Usually only for online multiplayer in paid games and cloud saves on some platforms. Free-to-play games often work without it. Single-player games work offline.

faq.q: Is a handheld gaming PC better than a console?
faq.a: It gives access to PC game stores and sales, and runs many games well at lower settings. It needs more setup, has shorter battery life in demanding games and not every game works perfectly. A console is simpler for most families.

title: How to choose a washing machine in 2026
lead: Pick the right drum size, an efficient energy class and a sensible spin speed. Most other features are nice to have, not essential.

p: Count people and laundry habits. As a guide: 1–2 people manage with 6–7 kg, 3–4 people with 8–9 kg, and larger families or people who wash bedding often with 10 kg or more. A bigger drum also lets you wash duvets at home.

Measure the space and the route to it. Standard freestanding machines are about 60 cm wide, 60 cm deep and 85 cm high. Slim models are 40–50 cm deep but usually hold less. Measure doorways and stairs, and leave a few centimetres behind for hoses. Decide between front-loading and top-loading; in Europe top-loaders are narrow (about 40 cm wide) and useful for tight spaces.

In the EU, the energy label uses a scale from A to G based on the Eco 40-60 programme. The label shows energy use per 100 cycles in kWh and water use per cycle in litres. Class A and B machines are now common, and many use around 45–55 kWh per 100 cycles. Compare these numbers rather than only the letter, because a bigger drum uses more in absolute terms.

Water use for an 8–9 kg machine is often 45–55 litres per Eco cycle. Remember that the Eco 40-60 programme is efficient because it is long, often three hours or more. Quick programmes save time but use more energy per kilo.

Spin speed sets how dry the clothes come out. 1,200–1,400 rpm is the sweet spot for most homes. 1,600 rpm removes a little more water and helps if you use a tumble dryer, but it creases clothes more and adds noise. The label also shows a spin-drying efficiency class from A to G.

The label shows spin noise in dB and a noise class from A to D. Around 70–74 dB in the spin phase is normal; below 72 dB is quiet. In an open-plan flat this matters more than a few extra rpm. Inverter (brushless) motors are usually quieter and more durable.

Most people use five or six programmes. Make sure you have Eco 40-60, a quick wash, wool or hand wash, synthetics and a hygiene programme at 60 °C or higher. Steam options help refresh clothes and reduce creases. Automatic detergent dosing saves detergent and effort if you wash often.

Delay start helps you use cheaper night-time electricity or solar power. Wi-Fi control is useful mainly for remote start and finished-cycle alerts. Check spare-part availability and warranty length: EU rules require many spare parts to be available for at least 10 years.

A washer-dryer saves space but usually dries only about half the washing load at once, takes a long time and uses more energy and water than a separate heat-pump dryer. If you have room for a stack, a washing machine with a dryer on top is usually better.
If you rent or move often, a freestanding machine is easier to take with you than an integrated one. Integrated models hide behind a kitchen door but cost more and are limited to about 60 cm width.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Do not pay extra for dozens of programmes you will never use. Antibacterial or "allergy" claims mostly mean higher temperature or longer rinses. A huge drum is wasted if you always run half loads. Big touch screens add cost and can be harder to repair than simple dials.

Finally, think about installation. Most retailers can deliver, connect and remove your old machine; make sure the floor is level and that the transit bolts are removed before the first wash, or the machine will shake and may be damaged.

checklist: Drum size fits your household (7–9 kg for most)
Fits the space and the route to it
Energy class A or B, check kWh per 100 cycles

faq.q: What size washing machine do I need?
faq.a: For one or two people, 6–7 kg is enough. Families of three or four are best served by 8–9 kg, and larger families by 10 kg or more. Bigger drums also handle duvets and bulky items.

faq.q: Why does the Eco programme take so long?
faq.a: It saves energy by washing at a lower temperature for longer, letting detergent do more of the work. A cycle of three hours or more is normal. It still uses far less electricity than a short hot wash.

faq.q: Is 1,600 rpm better than 1,400 rpm?
faq.a: It leaves clothes slightly drier, which helps if you use a dryer. The difference is small, and higher speeds add noise and creases. For most homes 1,400 rpm is enough.

faq.q: How long should a washing machine last?
faq.a: A well-maintained machine typically lasts 8–12 years. Clean the filter and detergent drawer regularly and run a hot cleaning cycle monthly. Spare-part availability and a good warranty help keep it running longer.

title: How to choose a tumble dryer in 2026
lead: A heat-pump dryer costs more up front but uses far less electricity. Check capacity, energy use per 100 cycles, condensation class and noise.

p: Match the dryer to your washing machine. The dryer should hold at least as much as the washer, ideally 1 kg more, because dry clothes need space to tumble. For most households 8 kg is right; large families may want 9–10 kg.

Check where it goes. Standard dryers are about 60 cm wide and 60–65 cm deep. Many can sit on top of a front-loading washing machine with a stacking kit. Condenser and heat-pump dryers need no outside vent, but they need some air around them, and a heat-pump dryer works best in a room above about 10 °C.

Think about how much you really dry. A household that runs four or more loads a week benefits most from the best efficiency and a larger drum. If you dry only towels and bedding in winter, a smaller and simpler heat-pump model is enough.

Heat-pump dryers recycle heat and run at lower temperatures. They typically use about half or less of the energy of a classic condenser dryer and are gentler on fabrics. Cycles are longer: a full cotton load often takes 2.5–3.5 hours.

Classic condenser and vented dryers are cheaper to buy but expensive to run. In the EU, strict efficiency rules since July 2025 have made heat-pump models the norm. In the US, vented electric and gas dryers are still common; ventless heat-pump models are growing and suit apartments without a vent.

Since July 2025 the EU dryer label uses an A to G scale, with energy use shown in kWh per 100 cycles, the same style as washing machines. Older stock may still show the previous A+++ to D label, so compare the kWh figures, not just the letters. If you dry several loads a week, the saving of a heat-pump dryer over its life can easily exceed the price difference.
Spinning clothes at 1,400 rpm or more in the washing machine shortens drying time and cuts energy use.

The condensation efficiency class shows how much moisture ends up in the water tank instead of the room. Class A means at least 90%; class B is acceptable; lower classes can make a small room humid. Look for a drain-hose option if you hate emptying the tank.

Typical noise is 62–66 dB. Under 64 dB is quiet enough for an open-plan home. Useful features include a moisture sensor that stops when clothes are dry, an anti-crease phase at the end, a wool or delicates programme, and delay start. A self-cleaning condenser saves you from rinsing it by hand.

Clean the lint filter after every cycle and the second filter or condenser regularly, as the manual describes. Blocked filters make cycles longer and increase energy use. Check that replacement filters are easy to buy.

Heat-pump dryers can be a little sensitive to being moved. After delivery, let the dryer stand upright for a few hours before the first use, as the manual usually advises, so the refrigerant and oil in the heat pump settle.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: "Quick dry" programmes usually handle only small loads. Steam refresh is nice but rarely replaces ironing. App control mainly gives you a finish alert. Do not compare cycle times between brands without checking the load size used for the claim.

Integrated or built-under dryers exist but have fewer choices and often lower capacity. A well-placed freestanding heat-pump dryer is usually the most flexible option. If you dry outdoors in summer and only use the dryer in winter, a mid-range model is fine; daily users should invest in efficiency and a good warranty.

faq.q: Is a heat-pump dryer worth it?
faq.a: Yes for most people who dry more than a couple of loads a week. It uses roughly half the energy of a condenser dryer or less, so the higher price is usually recovered over its lifetime. It is also gentler on clothes.

faq.q: Why does a heat-pump dryer take so long?
faq.a: It dries at a lower temperature to save energy and protect fabrics. A full load of cottons often takes 2.5–3.5 hours. Spinning clothes at a higher speed first shortens the cycle.

faq.q: Can I put a dryer on top of my washing machine?
faq.a: Usually yes, with a stacking kit made for the two machines. Both should be the same width and the washer should be front-loading. Check the manufacturer's list of compatible kits.

faq.q: Does a condenser dryer need a vent?
faq.a: No. Condenser and heat-pump dryers collect water in a tank or drain it through a hose. They need some ventilation around them, but no hole in the wall.

title: How to choose a fridge freezer in 2026
lead: Get the size right, check real energy use in kWh per year, and decide how much freezer space and noise you can live with.

p: Think about how you shop and cook. As a guide, 1–2 people manage with 200–250 litres in total, 3–4 people with 300–350 litres, and larger families with 400 litres or more. If you batch-cook or buy frozen food in bulk, size the freezer generously: about 50 litres per person is a comfortable figure.

Measure the space carefully: width, depth with the door, height, and room for the door to open past 90 degrees so drawers can come out. A standard combi is 60 cm wide and 180–200 cm tall; American-style side-by-side models are around 90 cm wide. Leave the ventilation gap the manual asks for.

In the EU, the label runs from A to G and shows annual consumption in kWh. Classes were reset in 2021, so a class C or D fridge today is often as good as an old A+++. A typical 60 cm combi uses about 100–250 kWh per year: class A and B models sit at the low end, class E at the high end.

A fridge runs every hour of every year, so the annual kWh figure multiplied by your electricity price shows the real yearly cost. An inverter compressor runs more evenly and is usually quieter and more efficient.

Placement affects consumption too. Keep the fridge away from the oven, radiators and direct sun, leave the recommended gap at the back and top, and set the fridge to about 4 °C and the freezer to −18 °C. Each degree colder adds a few percent to energy use.

No Frost freezers do not build up ice, so you never need to defrost them. Total No Frost covers the fridge section too. Static (low-frost) designs can keep food moister but need occasional defrosting. Multi-airflow systems keep the temperature even across shelves.

A crisper drawer with humidity control and a 0 °C zone keep vegetables, meat and fish fresh for longer. Check the climate class if the fridge will stand in a hot kitchen or a garage: class ST works up to 38 °C, class T up to 43 °C, and SN covers cold rooms down to 10 °C.
In open-plan homes, noise matters. Look for 35–38 dB for a quiet model; above about 40 dB the hum is easy to hear in a silent room. The EU label shows noise in dB and a class from A to D.

Bottom-freezer models are the most popular because the fridge sits at eye level. Check door storage for tall bottles, adjustable glass shelves, and whether the door hinge can be swapped to open the other way. Water and ice dispensers are convenient but often need a water connection and reduce usable space.

The EU label shows the freezer as a four-star compartment if it can freeze fresh food at −18 °C. Look at the freezing capacity in kilograms per 24 hours if you freeze large batches; 4–8 kg is common. Drawers made of clear plastic help you see what you have, and a fast-freeze function protects food that is already frozen when you add fresh items.
Check how long the freezer stays cold during a power cut. Many models keep food frozen for 15–24 hours if you keep the door shut, which matters in areas with unreliable supply.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Gross capacity is larger than usable (net) capacity; always compare net litres. Smart screens and cameras add cost and parts that can fail. "Antibacterial" linings make little real difference compared with regular cleaning. A great energy letter on a huge fridge can still mean higher kWh than a smaller model.

faq.q: What size fridge freezer do I need?
faq.a: A rough guide is 200–250 litres for one or two people, 300–350 litres for three or four, and 400 litres or more for bigger families. Adjust the freezer share to how much frozen food you keep.

faq.q: Is a class D fridge bad?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The scale was reset in 2021, and many good combis sit in classes C to E. Look at the annual kWh figure to compare real running costs.

faq.q: Can I put a fridge in the garage?
faq.a: Only if its climate class matches. In a cold garage, choose a model rated SN; in a hot one, choose ST or T. Otherwise the freezer may thaw or the compressor may overwork.

faq.q: How quiet is a quiet fridge?
faq.a: Around 35–38 dB is quiet enough for an open-plan living space. Above 40 dB you will notice the hum at night. Inverter compressors usually help.

title: How to choose a coffee machine in 2026
lead: Choose the machine type first: capsule, filter, manual espresso or bean-to-cup. Then check the grinder, milk system, cleaning and real cost per cup.

p: Ask three questions. What do you drink: espresso, milk drinks or long filter coffee? How many cups a day? And how much effort do you want to put in each morning?

Capsule machines are fast and clean but have the highest cost per cup and create waste. Filter (drip) machines make several mugs at once cheaply. Manual espresso machines give the best results for the money if you enjoy learning, but need a separate grinder. Bean-to-cup (fully automatic) machines grind, tamp and brew at the press of a button and suit people who want fresh espresso drinks with little effort.

Good espresso needs about 9 bar at the coffee. Labels with 15, 19 or 20 bar describe the maximum pump pressure, not the brewing pressure, so higher is not better. What matters more is stable temperature. On manual machines, PID temperature control keeps brewing water steady; a thermoblock heats up in under a minute, while a traditional boiler takes longer but holds temperature well for several drinks in a row.
Power of 1,300–1,500 W is typical. Very quick heat-up is useful if you make a single cup in the morning.

For filter machines, look for certification from a coffee association or a stated brewing temperature of 92–96 °C, a shower head that wets the grounds evenly and a thermal jug instead of a hot plate, which slowly burns the coffee.

Fresh grinding makes the biggest difference to taste. In bean-to-cup machines, look for several grind settings and a ceramic or steel burr grinder; ceramic burrs run cooler and quieter. A bean hopper of 200–300 g is enough for a few days. A bypass chute for pre-ground coffee is handy for decaf.
For manual espresso, budget for a proper burr grinder. A cheap blade grinder cannot grind fine and even enough for espresso.
Store beans in an airtight container away from light, and buy amounts you will use within two to four weeks of roasting. Even the best machine cannot rescue stale beans.

If you drink cappuccinos or lattes, the milk system matters as much as the espresso. A steam wand gives the best texture once you learn it. Automatic systems with a milk jug or tube make one-touch drinks but need cleaning after every use. Check that milk parts are dishwasher-safe and that the machine runs an automatic rinse.

All machines need descaling; how often depends on your water hardness. A water filter cuts descaling and improves taste. On bean-to-cup machines, a removable brewing unit that you can rinse under the tap makes hygiene easier; non-removable units rely on cleaning programmes and tablets.
A water tank of 1.5–2 litres saves constant refilling. Check the height under the spout for your favourite cup and the depth of your worktop space, including room to open the top for beans and water.

Think about noise as well. Grinders are the loudest part, often 70–80 dB for a few seconds, which can wake others in a small flat early in the morning. Some machines let you pre-set a quieter grind or use pre-ground coffee when needed.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Pump pressure numbers above 15 bar say nothing about taste. Dozens of preset drinks are mostly variations of the same espresso and milk. Big touch screens and apps are convenient but add cost and repair risk. For capsule machines, the real cost is in the capsules, so compare price per cup over a year.
