faq.q: How many bar does a good espresso machine need?
faq.a: About 9 bar at the coffee is the standard for espresso. Machines advertise 15–20 bar because that is the maximum pump pressure. Temperature stability and a good grind matter more than a higher bar figure.

faq.q: Bean-to-cup or capsule machine?
faq.a: Capsules are simpler and faster, but cost much more per cup and create waste. A bean-to-cup machine costs more to buy, but each cup is cheaper and the coffee is ground fresh. If you drink two or more cups a day, bean-to-cup usually pays off.

faq.q: How often should I descale?
faq.a: Follow the machine's indicator, which is usually every one to three months depending on water hardness. A water filter can stretch this. Skipping descaling hurts taste and shortens the machine's life.

faq.q: Do I need a separate grinder?
faq.a: For a manual espresso machine, yes, and a good one makes a big difference. Bean-to-cup machines have a built-in grinder. Filter machines work fine with pre-ground coffee, though fresh grinding still tastes better.

title: How to choose an air conditioner in 2026
lead: Size the unit to the room, compare SEER and SCOP efficiency, check indoor noise and plan proper installation. Split units beat portable ones.

p: Decide what you want: cooling only, or cooling and heating. Modern split air conditioners are air-to-air heat pumps and can heat a home efficiently in mild and even cold winters. Note which rooms you want to treat and whether you rent or own; a split unit needs drilling and an outdoor unit, so landlords and building rules may apply.

Split systems are far more efficient and quieter than portable units. Portable air conditioners with one exhaust hose are a stop-gap: they pull warm air into the room through gaps and use much more electricity for the same cooling. Multi-split systems run several indoor units from one outdoor unit.

Cooling power is shown in kW or BTU per hour (1 kW ≈ 3,412 BTU/h). As a starting point for a room with normal ceilings and average insulation: 2.5 kW (9,000 BTU) for about 15–25 m², 3.5 kW (12,000 BTU) for 25–35 m², 5 kW (18,000 BTU) for 35–50 m², and 7 kW (24,000 BTU) for 50–70 m².

Go up a size for top-floor flats, large south- or west-facing windows, high ceilings or a hot climate. Do not oversize too much: an oversized unit cools quickly but switches on and off, removes less humidity and wastes energy. A good installer should calculate the load for your room.

Ceiling height also counts: the guide above assumes about 2.5–2.7 m. For a 3 m ceiling, calculate by volume and add roughly 10–20%. Kitchens and rooms with many people or computers need extra capacity because they produce their own heat.

SEER measures seasonal cooling efficiency; SCOP measures seasonal heating efficiency. Higher is better. On the EU label, A+++ needs a SEER of 8.5 or more and a SCOP of 5.1 or more. Good units in 2026 reach SEER 7–9 and SCOP 4.5–5.2. If you plan to heat with the unit, SCOP matters as much as SEER. Check the heating capacity at low outdoor temperatures, such as −7 °C or −15 °C, if your winters are cold.
In the US, look at SEER2 and HSPF2 ratings and ENERGY STAR certification. All good units now use inverter compressors that adjust their speed instead of switching on and off.

Indoor units are quiet at low speed: look for 19–22 dB at the lowest setting for a bedroom, and around 35–40 dB at high speed. Outdoor unit noise matters for you and the neighbours; 45–50 dB is reasonable. Useful comfort features include a sleep mode, airflow that can be directed away from people, a dehumidify mode and washable filters.

Most split units use R32, which has a much lower climate impact than the older R410A. Some newer models use R290 (propane), with an even lower impact. EU rules on fluorinated gases are tightening, so a lower-impact refrigerant is a sensible choice for a long-lived unit.

Installation is not a DIY job. In the EU, only certified technicians may handle refrigerant. Poor installation causes leaks, noise and lower efficiency. Ask for vacuum testing of the pipes, a proper condensate drain and a solid mounting for the outdoor unit, and keep the paperwork for the warranty.

Ask how the condensate water will drain and where the pipes will run. Short, neat pipe runs improve efficiency. Plan for a service every one to two years, and clean the indoor filters every few weeks in heavy use.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: Ionisers and "plasma" air cleaning add little; a clean filter matters more. Maximum efficiency figures under ideal conditions are not the seasonal SEER or SCOP. Wi-Fi control is useful for pre-cooling a room before you arrive, but it is not essential.

faq.q: What size air conditioner do I need for a 20 m² room?
faq.a: Usually 2.5 kW (about 9,000 BTU) is enough for a 20 m² room with average insulation and normal ceilings. Choose 3.5 kW for a top floor, big sunny windows or a very hot climate. An installer can confirm with a load calculation.

faq.q: Can an air conditioner heat my home?
faq.a: Yes. A split air conditioner is an air-to-air heat pump and can heat very efficiently, often giving 4–5 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity. Check SCOP and heating output at low outdoor temperatures.

faq.q: Are portable air conditioners any good?
faq.a: They work for occasional use or where you cannot install a split unit. They are much less efficient and noisier, and single-hose models pull warm air back into the room. For daily summer use, a split system is far better.

faq.q: Can I install a split air conditioner myself?
faq.a: Generally no. Connecting the refrigerant circuit requires certification in the EU and similar rules apply elsewhere. DIY installation can void the warranty and cause leaks.

title: How to choose a gas boiler in 2026
lead: Choose combi or system type for your home, size it by heat demand and hot water, and insist on good controls and a registered installer.

p: Count bathrooms and people, and think about how often two taps run at once. A combi boiler heats water on demand with no tank and suits flats and homes with one bathroom. A system boiler heats a hot-water cylinder and suits homes with two or more bathrooms or several showers used at the same time. Heat-only (regular) boilers work with older systems that have tanks in the loft.

Before choosing, check local rules and incentives. Several European countries are restricting new fossil-fuel heating, especially in new buildings, and subsidies increasingly favour heat pumps. If your home is well insulated, ask an installer to compare an air-to-water heat pump as well.

Also consider space and the flue route. Combi boilers fit in a kitchen cupboard; a system boiler needs room for a cylinder of about 120–250 litres. Moving a boiler to a new location adds to the installation cost, so ask for a full quote.

sections.h: Output: kW for heating and hot water
p: Most homes need much less heating power than boiler sizes suggest. A flat often needs 5–10 kW for heating; a typical family house 10–20 kW. For combi boilers, the hot-water output sets the size: about 24–28 kW suits one bathroom, and 30–35 kW suits a larger bathroom or two that are not used at the same time.

Hot-water flow rate tells you how strong a shower will be. A 24 kW combi gives roughly 13–14 litres per minute at a 25 °C temperature rise; 30 kW gives about 17 and 35 kW about 20. Your incoming mains water pressure and flow must also be good enough, so ask the installer to measure them.

All new gas boilers sold in the EU and UK are condensing boilers with seasonal efficiency of around 92–94%. They only reach that when return water is cool, ideally below about 55 °C. Setting a lower flow temperature and using larger radiators or underfloor heating lets the boiler actually condense.

Modulation describes how low the boiler can turn down. A ratio of 1:7 to 1:10, with a minimum output of 3–4 kW, means the boiler can run gently in mild weather instead of switching on and off. That saves gas and reduces wear.
Seasonal efficiency is shown on the ErP energy label, usually as class A for a condensing gas boiler. Adding a compatible smart or weather-compensating control can raise the system's overall rating.

Good controls save more than small differences in boiler efficiency. Weather compensation adjusts water temperature to the outdoor temperature; load compensation adjusts it to how warm the room is. Look for thermostats that use a modulating protocol such as OpenTherm or the manufacturer's own, not simple on/off control. Thermostatic radiator valves let you set each room separately.

A gas boiler must be installed only by a registered or licensed gas installer, such as Gas Safe in the UK or the licensed installer required in your country. Never attempt DIY gas work. The installer should check the flue, gas supply, ventilation and pressure, and give you a commissioning certificate.

Book an annual service; most warranties require it. Fit a carbon monoxide alarm in rooms with gas appliances and near bedrooms. Warranty length varies widely, often from 2 to 10 years, so compare the terms, not just the headline number.

sections.h: What to ignore and marketing traps
p: "Hydrogen-ready" usually means the boiler can burn a gas blend with up to 20% hydrogen; it does not future-proof your heating. Bigger is not better: an oversized boiler cycles more and wastes gas. Apps are useful, but a basic weather-compensation setup often saves more.

faq.q: What size combi boiler do I need?
faq.a: For a flat or house with one bathroom, 24–28 kW is usually enough. For a large bathroom with a power shower, or two bathrooms not used at once, 30–35 kW is typical. A system boiler with a cylinder is better if showers run at the same time.

faq.q: Combi or system boiler?
faq.a: A combi heats water on demand and saves space, ideal for smaller homes. A system boiler stores hot water in a cylinder, so several taps can run at once. Homes with two or more bathrooms usually do better with a system boiler.

faq.q: Can I install a gas boiler myself?
faq.a: No. Gas work must be done by a registered or licensed installer by law in most countries. Faulty installation can cause gas leaks or carbon monoxide poisoning and will void the warranty.

faq.q: Should I choose a heat pump instead?
faq.a: In a well-insulated home, a heat pump can cut running costs and emissions, and it often qualifies for subsidies. It works best with low flow temperatures and larger radiators or underfloor heating. Ask an installer for a heat-loss calculation to compare both options.
